The problem, as the article pointed out, is that every major manufacturer of smart watches is trying to do one thing: treat it as the "Next major computing platform"

The only company that didn't do this was Pebble. They treated it as a watch first, a phone accessory second, and everything else a distant, community driven (but supported) third.

The demise of pebble was that the entire electronics industry decided to treat smartwatches like mini-phones, so they pitched them on all of the same features - processor speed, touchscreens, huge displays, "apps" and lifestyle. They tried to create a new niche, like smartphones and tablets did to sell a "solution" not a watch. That is why pebble failed - because the product they produced couldn't compete with the arbitrary metrics of the "mini-phone".

The workout watches don't treat them as such either (Garmin and Tomtom specifically). My guess is this is because they are coming from a different angle as a company. I have a Garmin watch that I freaking love, but it is mostly used for tracking my heartrate and GPS during workouts. I also wear it around daily as a normal watch, but I wouldn't buy one of these if that was all I used it for. It has notifications so I don't have to pull my phone out of my pocket to see who is calling or texting, so it is a little smart at least. Battery life is ~7 days so it isn't at risk of just dying on me.

Is it for everybody? No certainly not. I run or ride my bike daily and get great use out of it.

Would I buy an Apple or Android watch? Fuck no.
